title: Irregular potentials: 見える and 聞こえる
summary: 見られる and 聞ける are the regular potentials; 見える and 聞こえる are forced self-move forms that mean "look like" and "sound like".

blocks.text: Japanese is very regular. The few irregularities are local: a verb that is regular almost everywhere and bends in one spot. 見る and 聞く are two of them, and the bend has a reason.

The ichidan potential is **られる** and the godan potential is **え-stem + る**. 見れる, with the ら dropped, is a common speech habit (ら抜き). Many people still treat it as incorrect, and the course says to keep 見られる in your own writing. It is not a new verb.

Potentials are mostly **self-move**: 本が読める, "the book does readable". But the regular 見られる and 聞ける can also be other-move in describing clauses: さくらを見られる日 ("the day I can see Sakura") has an object. The irregular **見える** and **聞こえる** can only be self-move. They cannot take an object.

A small shade of meaning separates them from their regular partners. 見える is physical ability: it comes into view. 見られる suggests having the opportunity. If the tall lady in front takes off her hat, 芝居が見える. If tickets are on sale, 芝居が見られる.
Why they survive: looks like, sounds like

The real reason they exist is that **how something looks or sounds** is always self-move: it is the thing that appears, not something we do to it. So the forced forms became the "looks like / sounds like" verbs. A noun takes **に**, an い-adjective takes the **く-stem**.

blocks.en: That cloud looks like a dog.

blocks.jp: その話は変に聞こえる。
遠くから鐘の音が聞こえる。
blocks.en: A bell can be heard from far away.

items: Regular potentials: **見られる** (ichidan), **聞ける** (godan); 見れる is spoken ら抜き.
**見える** and **聞こえる** are forced self-move: no object.
**Nに見える**, **く-stem + 見える**, **Nに / adverb + 聞こえる** = looks / sounds like.
見える is physical visibility; 見られる suggests having the chance.

questions.note: Ichidan verbs take られる; 見える is the irregular, self-move form.

options: They are forced self-move: no object
questions.note: How things look or sound is always self-move.

questions.instruction: Which is the spoken ら抜き form of 食べられる?
questions.note: Dropping the ら gives the spoken 食べれる; keep 食べられる in writing.

questions.instruction: Which is the regular potential of 書く?
questions.note: Godan potential: え-stem + る.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap
questions.note: A noun takes に before 見える to say "looks like".
questions.en: That cloud looks like a fish.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap
questions.prompt: このかばんは新し＿＿見える。
questions.note: An い-adjective takes its く-stem before 見える.

questions.instruction: Which sentence means "I can hear music"?
questions.note: 聞こえる has no object: the music is the carriage with が.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap
questions.prompt: その音は雨の音＿＿聞こえる。
questions.note: Nに聞こえる means "sounds like N".

questions.instruction: Why 見られる and not 見える here?
questions.prompt: 来月、あの映画が見られる。
options: It is about having the opportunity
questions.note: 見られる suggests the chance to see; 見える is physical visibility.
questions.en: I can see that movie next month.

questions.instruction: Which is the main carriage?
questions.note: 見える is self-move: the station is what comes into view.
questions.en: I can see the station from here.

questions.instruction: True or false: 聞こえる can take an object with を.
questions.note: It is forced self-move, so no object.

questions.instruction: True or false: 聞ける is the regular potential of the godan verb 聞く.
questions.note: 聞く is godan: え-stem + る gives 聞ける.

questions.instruction: The tall man in front sat down, so the stage is in view. Which verb fits?
questions.note: 見える is physical ability: it comes into view.

questions.instruction: What does く show in 楽しく聞こえる?
questions.prompt: その歌は楽しく聞こえる。
options: It is the く-stem of an い-adjective before 聞こえる
questions.note: い-adjectives use the く-stem before 見える / 聞こえる.

questions.instruction: Why do 見える and 聞こえる survive as irregular forms?
options: They are the "looks like / sounds like" verbs, always self-move
questions.note: How something looks or sounds is the thing that appears, not something we do.

questions.note: 聞こえる takes no object; the voice is the carriage.
questions.en: A dog's voice can be heard from far away.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that gives the "looks like" meaning with 見える
questions.note: A noun + に before 見える means "looks like".
questions.en: That cloud looks like a mountain.

questions.instruction: Tap the spoken ら抜き form
questions.note: 見れる is spoken; 見られる is the written form.
questions.en: I can see this character even though it is small.

questions.note: The く-stem goes before 聞こえる.

questions.note: 聞こえる takes が for what is heard.
